rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lexicographers’ gloss denotes incapacity: someone is powerless to act because he cannot discern how to undertake a task.
rows.anchor: This means that a person is powerless to do something and he is unable to understand how to undertake a task.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers accept that God created them the first time but doubt that He can recreate them.
rows.anchor: these people cannot dare say that the Almighty was powerless in creating the heavens and the earth the first time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi hears sarcasm: since first creation posed God no difficulty, recreation should be no harder, as an artist can redraw an illustration better the second time.
rows.anchor: If an artist can draw an illustration the second time better than the first

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next passage moves from the recording of deeds and words to Judgment and the criminals, their casting into Hell and mutual cursing, then to the blessings prepared for the righteous.
rows.anchor: In the succeeding verses, first the elaborate arrangement made by the Almighty in recording the deeds and words of a person is mentioned.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Doubts about reviving the dead and recording every hidden and open deed are two sides of one objection; verse 4 briefly answers both.
rows.anchor: Both these doubts are two sides of the same coin. For this reason, in verse 4 earlier both are briefly answered.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God created man, He knows even the thoughts in his heart, let alone his words and deeds; this answers doubt about how every act could be recorded for judgment.
rows.anchor: The verse says that it is God Who has created man and even what comes in his heart is also known to God, let alone his words and deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A creator must know every detail of his creatures; otherwise, Islahi argues, how could God arrange for their protection and sustenance? The cited Qur’anic question is at 67:14.
rows.anchor: If a Creator is not aware of all the minute details of His creatures, how can He make arrangements for their protection and sustenance?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warīd means the life vein and is a common Arabic idiom for extreme nearness; God’s knowledge and power encompass each person, seen and unseen.
rows.anchor: This is a very common Arabic idiom which is used to express extreme nearness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase is elliptical: customary brevity suppresses the words meaning one seated on the right and one on the left.
rows.anchor: This suppression is because of customary brevity of Arabic.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beyond knowing hearts, God appoints two angels to each person to preserve every utterance as part of the conclusive communication of truth.
rows.anchor: He has deputed two angels each on a person, one of whom sits on this right and the other on his left.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the verse names recorded speech, deeds are understood by mentioning the dominant element and omitting the secondary; recording actions is even more likely.
rows.anchor: the arrangement to note down deeds done by the hand and foot is even more likely to have been made.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Narratives describe divided duties: the right angel records a person’s good words and deeds, while the left records the bad.
rows.anchor: It is evident from narratives that there is division of labour between these two angels.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since religious testimony treats two witnesses as reliable, Islahi says God has appointed two angels for each person.
rows.anchor: the evidence of two witnesses is considered reliable in religion, the Almighty has deputed two angels each on a person.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The recording angels cannot access a person’s thoughts; only God knows the unseen, and He alone knows the thoughts of hearts while concealing His creatures’ faults.
rows.anchor: the thoughts of a person are not accessible to these angels. It is only God Who has knowledge of the unseen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has also arranged for a person’s limbs, including hands, feet, ears, and eyes, to testify before Him.
rows.anchor: the hands, feet, ears and eyes of a person will also bear witness before the Almighty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ears preserve what people say, eyes record what they see, and other God-given limbs likewise bear witness, making it foolish to doubt that God can know every word and deed.
rows.anchor: our ears and whatever we see is being recorded by our eyes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A verb is suppressed before idh according to Arabic usage; Islahi supplies an admonition such as “Remember” or “Keep in mind,” reflected in his translation.
rows.anchor: the suppressed verb would be one which is instrumental in warning the addressees.

rows.speaker: Al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī takes a different view of the verb suppressed before idh; Islahi rejects his view without specifying it here.
rows.anchor: Al-Zamakhsharī has adopted another view

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥaqq refers to the Day of Judgment, the certain and incontestable reality about which the Qur’an informs people and which they deny.
rows.anchor: refers to the Day of Judgement which the Qur’ ān is informing them about

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past tense conveys certainty: people should not think the Hereafter is distant, since the time left in life is all that remains before it arrives.
rows.anchor: The past tense used is to express its certainty. The implication is that people should not regard it to be far off; it is at hand.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A narration says that whoever dies has had his Day of Judgment; death begins the circumstances of the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: he who died his Day of Judgement has come

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Barzakh is a prelude to the Hereafter; at death the truth of faith and its outcome are witnessed, the disbelievers’ denied fate begins, and doubt is removed.
rows.anchor: The life of Barzakh after death is just a prelude to the Hereafter. It is with death that the circumstances of the Hereafter begin.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi allows the phrase to function as an expression of the situation.
rows.anchor: can be an expression of the situation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi also allows the phrase to function as a verbal expression; he gives no preference between the two analyses.
rows.anchor: they can also be a verbal expression.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb ḥāda yaḥīdu means to walk while evading the path.
rows.anchor: means to walk evading the path.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This aptly depicts desire-followers who evade the Hereafter despite its signs and arguments, because they do not want to tread the right path.
rows.anchor: If they lead a life while evading the Hereafter, it is not because arguments which are in its favour are not known to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The trumpet’s sounding brings the warned day; its past tense pictures certainty, and what people imagined as a long interval will seem to pass in a blink.
rows.anchor: This too because of its certainty has been expressed in the past tense so that it can be picturized before the eyes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the trumpet, each soul is brought before God, driven from behind by one angel and accompanied by a second angel in front bearing the record as witness.
rows.anchor: one angel will be driving it forward from behind and another will be in front of him having the record of his words and deeds and will act as a witness.

rows.speaker: our early scholars
rows.claim: The early scholars likewise interpreted the verse as one angel driving the soul and another bearing witness to its record.
rows.anchor: and our early scholars too have interpreted it thus.

rows.speaker: some people
rows.claim: Some identify one angel as both driver and witness; Islahi rejects this because the reading is unsupported by linguistic principles.
rows.anchor: Some people have regarded one and the same angel to be implied as the beckoner and as the witness

rows.speaker: some others
rows.claim: Some take an angel as the driver and the soul with its deeds as the witness; Islahi rejects this as artificial and contrary to the wording.
rows.anchor: Some others regard the one who drives forth as an angel and regard the soul and its deeds to be the witness.

rows.speaker: some others
rows.claim: Some identify these as the two record-keeping angels from 50:17–18; Islahi rejects this because both would then need to share witness status, with no reason for the difference.
rows.anchor: Some others have regarded these two angels to be the same two which were referred to in the previous verse
